When the psalm was written is settled three separate ways against one dissent. Adam Clarke observes that although the Hebrew copies ascribe it to David, the inscription is missing from manuscripts and from the old Greek, Syriac, Latin, Ethiopic and Arabic versions and from most of the ancient fathers; he judges it composed long after David’s days and thinks it most likely a thanksgiving for the escape from the general massacre planned by Haman under the king of Persia. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion by another road: the ascription is wanting in the Greek codices and in the ancient versions generally, so that it is not so much as established as a point of textual criticism, and its Aramaizing character and its delight, after the manner of later poetry, in all kinds of verbal play betray a modern origin. Charles Ellicott argues from a single word, preferring man to men in the second verse: one who could speak of the whole world as divided into two parts discloses a sense of isolation and exclusiveness that brings us far down from the time of the prophets, who held that division as an ideal of the future where this writer treats it as accomplished fact; and he adds that the rare form behind proud is itself considered a mark of later composition. John Calvin resists. He rejects the setting in the deportation, since the complaints suit the later persecutions equally well, and calls the escape of reading the psalm as prophecy a forced conjecture, since the prophets speak of things to come differently; but having defended the title he will not limit the psalm to David’s time either, taking it rather as celebrating in general every occasion on which God had succoured his Church.

What is being pictured shifts twice in five verses and the readers follow it differently. John Gill hears the swallowing of the earth that took Korah, or of the fish that took Jonah, or rather the ravenous beasts to which the wicked are compared. Charles Ellicott makes the allusion to Korah certain, since the same verb and adjective stand together there; he observes that the sudden transition from earthquake to flood is characteristic of this poetry. Adam Clarke keeps the earthquake, a chasm opening and a whole city swallowed alive in a moment. Matthew Henry prefers the beast, a lamb devoured by a lion, and traces the rising of the figures as itself a mark of a song of ascents. John Wesley reads the proud waters of enemies great in number and swelling in rage.

C.H. Spurgeon is exercised by the broken syntax of the opening. The sentence is abrupt and remains a fragment, and the many italics of the received version show the translators doing their best to patch it; perhaps it had better have been left in its broken grandeur, and he gives it so — had it not been the Lord, he was for us, let Israel say. Here are two ifs, he adds, and yet there is no if in the matter. Matthew Henry is struck by the human agency: it is no marvel that the roaring lion should seek to swallow us, but that men should thirst after the blood of men, a son after his own father’s, is a thing to wonder at, for man is a wolf to man and there are those whose tender mercies are cruel; and he adds that God sometimes lets the enemies of his people prevail very far, so that his own power may appear the more illustrious in the deliverance. Augustine of Hippo takes the title instead, a song of ascent made not by the feet of the body but by the affections of the heart, and sung sometimes as by one and sometimes as by many, because the many are one; the martyrs, he says, have sung it already, having escaped.
6:
Two figures follow each other within a verse and the readers account for the change differently. Keil and Delitzsch make the pairing deliberate: the enemies are conceived as beasts of prey on account of their bloodthirstiness, as the world empires are in the book of Daniel, and then as fowlers on account of their cunning. Adam Clarke finds the second image fine because it shows at one stroke the weakness of the people and the craft of their adversaries. C.H. Spurgeon marks the same movement, the boiling flood left behind for wild beasts whose teeth are prepared to tear. Charles Ellicott sees nothing more than another rapid transition to a favourite figure, that of the hunter’s net. Keil and Delitzsch add a point from the accents: the text does not say that the soul is like a bird which has escaped, but that the soul is as a bird, the escaping standing by itself.

On the teeth that did not close, Matthew Henry and C.H. Spurgeon draw the same inference in the same words. The enemies had no power over God’s people but what was given them from above, and they could not be a prey to those teeth unless God gave them up; Spurgeon adds that the more imminent the danger the more eminent the mercy, and that although the verse reads like a merely negative blessing no boon could be more positively precious. On the bird, John Gill presses the likeness for all it is worth — harmless, weak, fearful, and worthless, since the word means a sparrow — and makes the fowlers Satan and the men under his influence, from whose devices the birds escape only by a wisdom given them to discern the stratagem. Matthew Henry keeps the bird helpless throughout and puts the whole rescue in the last clause, since God breaks the snare and turns the counsel of the enemies into foolishness, as Isaac was saved when he already lay ready to be sacrificed. C.H. Spurgeon instead itemises the fowler’s methods, some decoyed by evil companions, some enticed by dainties, some driven in by hunger and some flying into the net out of pure fright.

Adam Clarke reads the whole psalm off one historical event and says so plainly. The snare had been laid completely and there was humanly no prospect of escape, until the providence that moved the king to call for the book of the records to be read to him, and the once very improbable advancement of the queen, broke the snare so that the bird escaped while the poacher was caught in his own trap and executed; the book that tells the story he calls probably the best comment on this psalm, and he guesses that its hero wrote it. He also notes that the Chaldee gives the closing clause as the name of the Word of the Lord, and takes that of the substantial Word, the person afterwards so termed, and not of a word spoken or a prophecy delivered. John Gill draws from the same clause that help is in the Lord only and in no creature. Matthew Henry observes that the singular of an earlier psalm has here become plural, personal help becoming the concern of the public, and argues that the God of Israel is the same who made the world and will therefore have a church in the world. C.H. Spurgeon ends on the same thought turned twice: he made heaven for us and will keep us for heaven, he made the earth and will succour us upon it until the hour comes for our departure.
